mercy_translation.text:
If, because he is not seen, people disbelieve that he has risen, it is time for those unbelievers also to deny what belongs to nature. For it belongs to God not to be seen, yet to be known from his works, as was said above.

If there are no works, then they rightly disbelieve in the One who is not visible. But if the works cry aloud and show the truth plainly, why do they deliberately deny the life of the resurrection that is so clearly manifested? Even if their minds have been blinded, they can at least with their outward senses see the undeniable power and divinity of Christ.

A blind person may not see the sun, yet by perceiving the warmth produced by it knows that the sun is above the earth. In the same way, those who argue against the truth—even if they do not yet believe and remain blind regarding it—should at least, from the power manifested in others who believe, not deny Christ's divinity and the resurrection accomplished by him.

For it is clear that if Christ were dead, he would not drive out demons and despoil idols; demons would not obey a dead man. But if they are manifestly driven away by the invocation of his name, it is clear that he is not dead. Especially because demons, seeing things not visible to human beings, would be able to know if Christ were dead and simply refuse to obey him.

But now the demons see what impious people do not believe: that he is God. Therefore they flee and fall before him, saying what they also spoke when he was in the body: “We know who you are: you are the Holy One of God,” and, “Leave us alone; what have you to do with us, Son of God? I beg you, do not torment me.”

Since demons confess and the works bear witness daily, it should be clear—and let no one be shameless before the truth—that the Savior raised his own body and is the true Son of God, existing from him as the Father's own Word, Wisdom, and Power. In later times, for the salvation of all, he took a body, taught the inhabited world concerning the Father, abolished death, and bestowed incorruption upon all through the promise of the resurrection, raising his own body as its firstfruits and displaying it through the sign of the cross as a trophy over death and its corruption.

translator_notes: Translated directly from the Greek source.
The analogy of a blind person recognizing the sun by its warmth supports Athanasius' argument from effects to an unseen cause.
The chapter summarizes Christ as Word, Wisdom, and Power of the Father and connects resurrection with universal incorruption.
